title: Text pair for Q1 to Q6: The Lens and Letter on the Railway
subject: English Language
source: Written for english-language/y10 lesson 54 (Text pair 'The Lens' (Text One) and 'Letter on the Railway' (Text Two), teacher-written (pupil PDF))
intro: Lesson 54: Two extracts under time: Q1 to Q6. Teacher-written for TGA. Read, then answer under time.

passage.title: Text One: The Lens
paras: The lighthouse keeper's cottage is a museum now. You pay at a little window and climb the same hundred and twelve steps he climbed each night, though nobody makes you do it in a gale. At the top, behind glass, sits the great lens: a beehive of prisms taller than a man, so clean it seems to hold the sky. A card explains how it turned on a bath of mercury, so smoothly that a child could push it. I did push it, very gently, when the guide was not looking. It moved. Somewhere, two hundred years of ships seemed to move with it.

passage.title: Text Two: Letter on the Railway
paras: Dear Mother, The railway has reached our town at last, and with it a noise I am not sure we shall ever grow used to. On Tuesday the first engine came in, breathing fire and steam like a creature from one of Father's old books. Half the town ran to the station; the other half ran away from it. The baker's horse broke its rope and was found two fields off, eating Mr Hale's cabbages. I confess I stood very near the platform's edge, and when the great wheels stopped I felt my heart had been running all the way from London with it.

questions.q: Q1. How many steps did the keeper climb each night?
Q2. What did the lens turn on?
Q3. How does the writer use language and structure to make the visit memorable?
questions.a: 'beehive of prisms'; 'hold the sky'; the secret push as turning point; the leap of 'two hundred years'.

questions.q: Q4. On which day did the first engine come in?
Q5. Give two effects of the engine's arrival on the town.
questions.a: Any two: half the town ran to the station; half ran away; the baker's horse broke its rope and fled.

questions.q: Q6. How does the writer use language and structure to present the railway's arrival?
questions.a: 'breathing fire and steam'; the balanced sentence of the divided town; the comic horse anecdote; 'confess'; the heart 'running all the way from London'.
Q1: a hundred and twelve. Q2: a bath of mercury.
Q4: Tuesday. Q5: any two: half the town ran to the station; half ran away; the horse broke its rope and fled.
